props.title: Desk Set

sections.content: Desk Set (1957) brilliantly captures the dawn of workplace automation, pairing Katharine Hepburn and Spencer Tracy in their eighth collaboration. As reference librarian Bunny Watson, Hepburn embodies the human intelligence that supposedly faces obsolescence from EMERAC, an early computer. The film remarkably predicts modern anxieties about AI replacing knowledge workers, while delivering sharp romantic comedy beats. It shares DNA with other workplace revolution films like Modern Times (1936) and Executive Suite (1954), but stands unique in celebrating female intellectual prowess in the male-dominated 1950s corporate world.

sections.content: The film's office setting provides fertile ground for exploring gender dynamics in mid-century corporate America. Like His Girl Friday (1940) and The Best of Everything (1959), it showcases professional women navigating male-dominated spaces. Hepburn's Bunny Watson runs her reference department with encyclopedic knowledge and quick wit, challenging both the machine meant to replace her and Richard Sumner's (Tracy) assumptions about automation's superiority. The film's progressive stance on women's intellectual capabilities was radical for 1957.

Director Walter Lang brings a light touch that balances workplace comedy with deeper questions about technology's impact on society. The massive EMERAC computer, while played for laughs, eerily foreshadows real concerns about automation and AI. Similar themes would later emerge in films like 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) and Computer Chess (2013), but Desk Set handles them with romantic comedy charm rather than dystopian dread. sections.content: Desk Set represents the mature phase of Tracy and Hepburn's legendary screen partnership. Their chemistry crackles with the ease of longtime collaborators, while the script gives them meaty material about knowledge, progress, and human connection. Unlike earlier pairings like Pat and Mike (1952) or State of the Union (1948), here they're intellectual equals facing modernization's challenges together rather than romantic antagonists.
